title: Stop AI Agent Hallucinations: 5 Techniques + Production Patterns - Elizabeth Fuentes, AWS
talk_summary: Elizabeth Fuentes (AWS) presents five code-level (not prompt-level) techniques to cut token waste and catch agent failures: semantic tool selection, GraphRAG for aggregation/count queries, multi-agent validation (executor/validator/critic), neuro-symbolic hooks that enforce rules in Python before tool calls, and runtime 'steering' guardians that let the agent self-correct instead of hard-blocking. All demos use the Strands agent framework with local vector stores, Neo4j, and a local steering server, with an AWS Bedrock AgentCore production mapping.

takeaways.technique: Semantic tool selection (retrieve top-k tool schemas per query)
takeaways.what_they_do: Embed tool descriptions in a local vector store, retrieve only the top-k (3) most relevant tool schemas per user query, and swap them into the agent's tool registry each invocation instead of sending all tool schemas every call.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the model sees only three most relevant tools. Tokens usage drops from thousands to fewer than 300
takeaways.numbers: 29 tools ~3,000 tokens/call of schemas; filtered to <300 tokens; ~2,000 tokens/query baseline

takeaways.what_they_do: For questions requiring counts, averages, or relationship traversal, replace vector-chunk retrieval with a structured graph query (Cypher) so the model gets a computed, verifiable answer rather than sampling top-k chunks and estimating.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Vector search always returns something even when nothing is truly relevant... It cannot aggregate, count, or traverse relationship across all the full data set. So, it estimates.

takeaways.what_they_do: Split act/check/approve into three agents with distinct system prompts chained via a swarm handoff, so a second and third agent catch fabricated success or tool errors the acting agent rationalized.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the executor gets the error, the validator catches, the critic rejects this, and the user never see a fabricator response

takeaways.technique: Neuro-symbolic guardians: rules in code via pre-tool-call hooks
takeaways.what_they_do: Implement hard constraints as Python hooks that fire before a tool executes, inspecting parameters and cancelling the call if a rule fails, rather than trusting the system prompt to enforce limits.
takeaways.evidence_quote: A rule in the prompt the model read it as a suggestion. A rule in the code the model can not escape it.
takeaways.numbers: Same model/tools/prompt: prompt-only agent confirmed booking without payment and exceeded guest limit; hook agent blocked both

takeaways.technique: Runtime steering guardians (soft rules that let agent self-correct)
takeaways.what_they_do: For soft constraints, instead of blocking, a hook fires and steers the model to an alternative (e.g. split a 50-guest booking into two rooms) so the task completes without user retry; rules live on a local server and are picked up on the next call without redeploying agent code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: with agent control, it steered the models and the task complete... rules are registered on a local server via API

takeaways.technique: Ground-truth query sets to measure technique impact
takeaways.what_they_do: Built a labeled set of 90 queries with known correct tool and compared baseline vs. filtered agent on token count and accuracy, making the cost/quality tradeoff measurable rather than asserted.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I have a ground truth because I know what is the best... the best tool to answer the question, so we can know if our agent is okay or not
